q: A resolver has an empty cache and looks up www.example.com. Which server gives it the final IP address?
options: A root server
The .com server
The domain's own (authoritative) server
The browser
why: The root points to the .com server, and the .com server points to the domain's own server. Only the authoritative server holds the real records.

q: Put the steps of a first lookup in order.
items: The resolver asks a root server and gets the .com server as a referral
The resolver asks the .com server and gets the domain's own server as a referral
The resolver asks the domain's own server and gets the record
The resolver saves the answer and gives the IP to the browser
why: Each server only points to the next one. The last one knows the answer. The resolver saves it for the TTL.

q: Which record type points one name at another name?
options: A
AAAA
CNAME
MX
why: A gives an IPv4 address, AAAA gives an IPv6 address, MX names the mail servers. CNAME says this name is another name for that one.

q: A resolver asks the domain's own server again on every single lookup.
why: It keeps the answer for the record's TTL. Until that time runs out, the answer comes from the cache and no server is asked.

q: A resolver is asked for a name that does not exist. Which answer code does it get? Type it in capital letters.
why: NXDOMAIN means no such name. Resolvers cache this too, for a time taken from the zone's SOA record, so a record you add later may not show up at once.

q: A record has a TTL of 300 and a resolver saved it at second 0. Which are true?
options: At second 299 the answer still comes from the cache
At second 300 the resolver asks the servers again
The TTL in a cached answer counts down
The authoritative server pushes a new value to the resolver when you change the record
why: The TTL is the time the resolver may keep the answer. Nothing is pushed. The resolver only asks again when its copy runs out.

q: Your A record has a TTL of 86400 (one day). You must move to a new server and want most users on it within minutes. What should you have done?
options: Nothing, DNS changes are instant
Lowered the TTL to 60 at least one old TTL (a day) before the move, then changed the IP
Raised the TTL to a week
Asked every resolver to flush its cache
why: Old copies live up to the old TTL. Lower the TTL first, wait one old TTL, then change the IP. After that every cache re-asks within a minute.

q: When you change a DNS record, the DNS system pushes the new value to every resolver. This is what propagation means.
why: Nothing is pushed. Each resolver keeps its own copy until its TTL ends and then asks again. Propagation is just all those copies running out.

q: Why can you not put a CNAME on the apex (example.com itself)?
options: CNAMEs are too slow at the top level
A CNAME must be the only record on its name, and the apex always has NS and SOA records
The root server forbids it
A CNAME needs a TTL of 0
why: RFC 1912 says a CNAME is not allowed to coexist with any other data. The apex always holds NS and SOA records, so it cannot be a CNAME.

q: You want example.com (the apex) to point at a hosting company's name. Which can work?
options: A Route 53 alias record
Cloudflare CNAME flattening
An A record with the host's IP address
A normal CNAME record at the apex
why: Route 53 alias and Cloudflare flattening are provider features that answer with IP addresses. An A record works if the IP is stable. A normal CNAME at the apex breaks the zone.

q: You add the record *.apps.example.com A <server IP> for CapRover and deploy a new app called shop. What happens?
options: shop.apps.example.com resolves to the server at once, but HTTPS still needs its own certificate
You must add a DNS record for shop first
shop.apps.example.com resolves and gets a wildcard certificate for free
Only apps.example.com resolves
why: A wildcard record answers for every name below it that has no record of its own. The CapRover docs say wildcard DNS does not create a wildcard TLS certificate.

q: A DNS wildcard *.apps.example.com can answer for a.b.apps.example.com, but a TLS wildcard certificate for *.apps.example.com does not cover that name.
why: DNS wildcards (RFC 4592) can match several labels when the names in between do not exist. A TLS wildcard covers exactly one label.

q: Which record type names the mail servers of a domain? Type the two letters in capitals.
why: MX records list the mail servers with a priority number. TXT records often hold things like SPF and verification strings.

q: DNS answers with 3 server IPs, and a health check removes one dead server from the answers. TTL is 3600. What is the problem?
options: None, users move to the other servers at once
Resolvers that saved the old answer can keep sending users to the dead server for up to an hour
DNS cannot do health checks at all
The dead server stays in the answers forever
why: Failover through DNS is only as fast as the TTL. That is why failover records use short TTLs, 60 seconds or less according to the Route 53 FAQ.
